utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning everyone. Good morning, Ms. West. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue with the witness, I would just like to put something on the record that happened since our last sitting and that is on Tuesday of last week we disclosed the identity of 17 of our witnesses by filing Rule 92 ter notifications, and on Friday I received an e-mail from one of those witnesses indicating that his family in Sarajevo had been threatened and he was no longer willing to testify. So we informed the Chamber and OTP of this and also reported it to the Victims and Witnesses Section. And on Friday I -- afternoon I met with the Victims and Witnesses Section protection officers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, sorry to interrupt you. Do you wish to continue in open session in the presence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we want the public to be aware -- want this to be a matter of public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not seeking specific remedy for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not in this case, but we're trying to deter this from happening again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. So we informed the protection officers of the Victims and Witnesses Section on Friday afternoon and they promised to follow-up on this matter. And we conducted our own investigation also over the weekend. As the Chamber knows, under Rule 77 interfering with the administration of justice and a witness is punishable by up to seven years' imprisonment and we had not had any single instance of interference or threat or intimidation during the Prosecution case, and we're concerned that in the first week of the Defence case we already have such an incident. And I wanted to nip it in the bud by serving notice at this time that such incidents would be taken very seriously. And we would ask the Chamber and the Prosecution as well as the Bosnian authorities for its full co-operation when such incidents occur. Thank you. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West. I forgot to inform you that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi away due to her urgent personal matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to go back to a couple of the things that we spoke about last week, and on Thursday in our discussion of proportionate fire you mentioned hospitals. And at transcript 29123 you said that you did not retaliate against hospitals because we were always afraid of inflicting major civilian casualties if we had done that. I then asked you whether there were other locations in the city that you considered completely off limits, and at the time you didn't answer my question so I'd like to try it again. Do you have any other examples like hospitals of locations that were off limits for firing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hospitals, bus stations, railway stations and rail lines, schools, and all the areas where larger groups of civilians tend to gather, those were the facilities that we didn't target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you say "all the areas where larger groups of civilians tend to gather," what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born and raised there, so I knew where bus stops were, where tram stations were, big supermarkets where people went to get their supplies, and wherever the frequency of the civilian population was quite high, those were the areas that we did not expose to fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so taking, for example, again the hospital, how near to the hospital would you consider a reasonable distance to fire at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we did not open fire at areas around hospitals, be it 500 metres or 1 kilometre. In general terms, areas around hospitals were not our firing targets. I already told you that the military hospital and Kosevo hospital were among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you just said "be it 500 metres or 1 kilometre," are you suggesting within --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So within 1 kilometre of a hospital, you would not fire within 1 kilometre around it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this distance would be applicable as well to all those other areas you mentioned, you spoke about railway stations, bus stations, areas where large groups of civilians tend to gather?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I understand that the reason you did this is because you did not want to potentially kill any civilians, but were there any circumstances where you would have accepted the risk of civilian deaths?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in such cases I wouldn't open fire if I thought that the civilian population was at risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On Thursday you spoke about preparation regarding firing at page transcript 29111. You said that there was simple preparation, abbreviated preparation, and full preparation. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's start with full preparation. Can you tell us what that includes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full preparation involves bulletins, the correct co-ordinations of the targets, topographic co-ordinations, and when you have all that you fire one or two shells to the target that you want to reach. But the preparation is rather long. You have to have the right temperature of the year, the right ammunition preparation, the charge, and the data must not be more than two hours old.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you said -- in the beginning you said you needed the correct co-ordinates of the targets, the topographic co-ordinates. Would you also need to know what the objective was? Besides just the geographical location, would you need to know what the objective of the target was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, this was done based on what I received from my observers or what I received from my superior command. They had to know what the objective was, was it a trench or a piece of weaponry, and based on that it would be decided what to do because you had to know what kind of weaponry was used on the other side, what kind of weaponry fire was being opened from by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us what abbreviated preparation included.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviated preparation excludes the air temperature, and if we couldn't do that we used a so-called simple preparation which involved topographic preparation. When you had that, you fired one or two shells and then you correct fire. If you managed to hit your target in the first go, then you didn't do anything. And in order to reach the target, you have to have an area around it of 50 metres. If you are within that range --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. I'm not sure that this sentence is correct: [In English] "If you managed to hit your target in the first go, then you didn't do anything." Then you didn't do anything. I think the witness didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you again. You were speaking about simple preparation and you said it involved topographic preparation. Tell us again what that included.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simple preparation means that you have to have all the elements from the topographic map, you fire a shell after you have calculated all the elements, and then you fire one shell towards the enemy and towards your target. A successful hit is anything within the range of 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So as I understand it, simple preparation just means having the location and then attempting to fire at that particular location?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to have a topographic map in a certain scale, 25.000 or 50.000, and you have to be precise when transferring all the elements. You have to know whether your observers have calculated the azimuth, the level of the observation line, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the other day when we were speaking about the type of fire that your unit would engage in, you told us that it was in all cases defensive retaliatory fire, you gave us one exception, but it was mostly retaliatory fire that had to be very quick. It that it was -- it took five to ten minutes to retaliate. In those cases were you referring to this type of preparation, simple preparation? Is that the type of preparation you employed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simple preparation can be done within the scope of five minutes, hence the term: Simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yet full preparation would take much longer; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full preparation takes much longer. You have to measure the air temperature, the gunpowder temperature, this must not be older than two hours. The temperature changes from let's say in the morning until the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I be of any help to say "metal [indiscernible]," metal means "metrological elements for the fire." The transcript so far didn't comprise this expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just so I'm absolutely clear, in the cases where you were firing in retaliation, in those situations you would use simple preparation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 23928.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a document from August 1994. It's from the corps command and it's an order for full combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told it was not released yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Mr. President. Can we have P01614, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is going to be the implementation order for the document that we will see in a moment. And if we can go to page 2, please, this is to the command of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, but on page 2 of this - and again it's August 1994 - under paragraph 9 we see: "Co-ordinate actions with the units of the 1st Mixed Artillery Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and plan fire at the eastern slopes ..." Mr. Skrba, that refers to your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here Major Goran and that's not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct. And the direction to Major Goran is to co-ordinate actions with your unit. Do you have a memory of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Again I understand that, sir. My question is: Do you have a memory in August of 1994 of this co-ordination for full combat-readiness?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I did not read this order and maybe at that time I was somewhere else in another part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we go to page 1 of this order, please. Even though you say you didn't receive this order, I just want to talk to you about some language in this order. It's already something that we've already addressed once. And under paragraph 1 it says: "I hereby order: "All 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade units and positions and in areas of disposition, MUP units in the zone of responsibility, work obligation units, and the population are to be placed at full b/g." And then it says: "At all costs stop possible enemy attacks on any section of the brigade's line of contact." Now, the other day we spoke about targeting language and you were saying that it has to be very specific, and you also spoke about proportionate fire. Would you agree with me that the phrase "at all costs" is very different than the proportionate fire that you spoke of adhering to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously "at all costs" means that in case of an enemy attack we shouldn't allow their passage through our area. So the means were different. Fire had to be more fierce. If we had such targets, we would fire a lot more than just one or two shells that we would fire in other situations when we wanted to avoid collateral damage. This is a different situation. This is a full enemy attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you just said "if we had such targets," but here it says: "At all costs stop possible enemy attacks ..." Here there aren't even actual targets, it's just possible targets. Is this type of language something that you would find to be appropriate and consistent with what you spoke about the other day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. However, if you find yourself in a situation when the enemy wants to break through our forward defence line, why else would we have been there if not to stop such an attempt.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, that's not responsive to my question. My question is: Do you find this language to be in keeping with what you described to us to be detailed targeted language at specific locations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was issued in a totally different segment of warfare. It refers to a possible enemy attack or a breakthrough. If the enemy wanted to break through our lines and enter our territory, and this is a completely different situation to the one that I described previously. It is not the same thing to open fire on the front line in order to interrupt the cease-fire on the one hand and to stop the enemy who is attempting to break through your forward defence lines. The two situations are completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's go to what we were speaking about the other day, which was specific targets. And when we ended on Thursday I had asked you to look at the map that I gave you and that was 65 ter 23918, and specifically we're looking at map 3. And when we ended off I asked you to take a look at this map and to tell us where the tank was located that you referred to in paragraph 18 of your statement. And, sir, if you can go to -- you can turn the page --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do it on this map too. Do you want this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There you go. That one.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank was below Hum and it moved around the curves depending on what it wanted to target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we will just ask the usher if he can turn on the screen so you can actually mark this on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that that's where the tank was located that you spoke about in paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was that tank located there throughout the entire war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I wasn't there. However, it opened fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 18 of your statement you said: "Velesici May 1992 a tank during the entire war ..." Was it located there during the entire war.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It opened fire from there in 1992, in 1993, in 1994, but I don't know whether it was stationed there all the time or perhaps it was moved to some other lines. When it did open fire, however, it opened it from this location.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. To make sure I understand, it's your testimony that when it opened fire it was located there, but you do not understand that it was actually located there throughout the entire war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it opened fire on Zlatiste and Vrace on our forward defence lines, that's where it fired from. I don't know whether it moved further away from here, downward, or somewhere else, I don't know. I wasn't there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just to be sure I understand what you're saying, at line 12 you said: "... I don't know. I wasn't there all the time." Did you say "I wasn't there all the time" or "it wasn't there all the time"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat for the thousandth time. I was not there in order to know whether it was there all the time; however, it opened fire from that location in 1992, in 1993, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During those same years, how often did you shoot at that tank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact figure, but perhaps seven or eight times -- six to eight times I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Over the course of 1992, 1993, 1994, and into 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention 1995 at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. My mistake. So three years. And obviously you failed to destroy it because you kept on shooting; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crew was good. The drivers were good I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to look at -- I want to review what type of targeting went on in Velesici to see what you knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P01522, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let me back up. Can you put your signature on this and give us a date. The date is October 22nd, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5935, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And now P01522.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another intercept between General Mladic and the gentleman Potpara. We saw an intercept between the two of them the other day as well. I know you're not a party to it, this intercept, but I want to ask you about it. So we have the B/C/S and I'll just read along in English and it will come up. In this they're on the phone and General Mladic says: "What's the news? "A. No news. "Mladic: Are you firing something? "A. No, I'm not firing anything. "Mladic: Is there shelling close to you? "A. No shelling close to me. "Where is the shelling going on? "A. I don't know. This way up towards the tobacco factory Pofalici. "Mladic: Have Velesici been shelled? "A. Yep. "Mladic: Have they been hit there? "A. Yes, they have. "There will be more of it there. "A. All right." Now, I'm just going to stop there. When Mladic said "has Velesici been shelled," this is in the past tense, but this is a period of time, end of May 1992, in which you were involved, what would have been the target in Velesici?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't say what target is at stake on the basis of this interception, but if that's the 29th, then I know that Velesici was shelled and over 80 per cent of the population was civilian and there were Serbians. Then there were attempts on the part of the Muslim forces to drive out the Serbs and to take territory if it happened during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So would you agree that this language suggests that there is no specific target other than the town itself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree. I'm not familiar with the conversation that concerns opening fire, the target, the reasons for which fire was opened. On the basis of this intercept, it's not possible for me to draw any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I'd like to go to the day before to see if we can get any more information about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can I have P1521, and this is May 28th. And if I can have page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another intercept between Mladic and Mirko Vukasinovic. And in the first page they're just sort of handling introductions, but when we get to the second page Mladic sayings: "Do not shell the barracks. Can you reach Velesici? "A. Yes. "Do you have a gun pointed at some target there? "Yes, I do. "Mladic: You do or you do not? "A. I do. "Mladic: How soon can you fire? "A. Well, I could fire in five or ten minutes, no sooner than that. "Mladic: Tell me, can you shell Bascarsija? "Yes, I can." And then Mladic says: "I beg your pardon." Sir, again, you're not privy to these conversations, but nonetheless you've told the Court that also you were responsible for targeting a tank in the same area for three years. Can you agree with me that at least from this conversation it appears that General Mladic has no information on any particular target, only some target?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree because they can probably see Velesici and see whether there's any fighting there. They didn't ask for that part of the town to be shelled for no reason. There must have been some kind of reason for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go to the next town or section of town that you mentioned in your paragraph 18, and if we can go back to 65 ter 23918, we will go to map 5, which is Ciglane. So you can turn the page --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can use this too.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But if you turn the page you'll get a bigger -- there you go. Now, this is the area on the other side of the tunnel from Velesici; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the town in the direction of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we don't need to do this in e-court, but if you just turn your page you're going to see a satellite version of this same town. Do you see that? We don't need to do it in e-court. And looking at those two maps, can you tell us what the general nature of the area was? Was it a residential area? Was it an industrial area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a residential area exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you can go back to the map we see on the screen right now, I think you had mentioned -- strike that. Was there a hospital in Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by the entrance of the tunnel from which the tank would come out there was no hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So if we can stop there on e-court, and I'll direct your attention to the number 81 which is in the middle of the screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And perhaps e-court can focus in on that 81 and that 126 in red numbers. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, that's the area of the hospital and the college of medicine; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness mumbled something but it was not audible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you want me to say. What sort of answer would you like? What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question was -- regarded a hospital, and my question was: In the area of -- you see the numbers 81 and 126. To your knowledge is that the area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that where the hospital was located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital is 71 and this location has been marked as 81, the medical faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And I think in fact there are two hospitals. You're correct. There's a 71 up in the corner of this map which is also a hospital, but do you remember 81 also being a hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the main part.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was the medical faculty there. As to whether there was a hospital in the medical faculty, I don't know. It's possible, they could have done all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 19, line 19 is the answer. It's not part of the question which what the transcript would lead one to believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to go back to something you just said. When I started talking about this hospital, you said: "Well, by the entrance of the tunnel from which the tank would come out there was no hospital." When you say "entrance of the tunnel the tank would come out," tell us a little bit more about that. Was the tank parked inside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank was in the tunnel; that is certain. The tank that they had seized from the French [as interpreted], the self-propelled gun.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make a correction. They seized the self-propelled gun from the French. They didn't seize the tank from the French, only the self-propelled gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of overlapping, the interpreters didn't get it right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the witness said that they seized the self-propelled gun from the French. That wasn't transcribed. It seemed as if it was the tank that had been seized from the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was, it was transcribed, but it was not correctly transcribed because of your intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, could you repeat your answer, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came out of the tunnel, the tank, especially in 1991, and later the self-propelled gun seized from the French, but they were parked in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This tank that you're describing, is this the same tank that you noted in -- earlier in Velesici that you indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. I think it's a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. How often in your time in Sarajevo did you shoot at the tank in Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, six to eight times as was the case in Velesici during these three or four years, but in 1994 and 1995 it's the French tank --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That went into action more frequently while they had ammunition and shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you shot at that tank, you made sure that there were no civilians around; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I had a look to make sure there weren't any civilians, but the tank, when the tank goes into action they all flee -- I mean when their tank goes into action.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 18 this was the only target that you mention in Ciglane. Were there other targets in Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any other targets. I didn't fire on any other targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P0820, please, and for e-court that will be page 59.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard some evidence from a senior United Nations military officer who said or confirmed at paragraph -- e-court page 59, please. Confirmed at paragraph 197 that in June of 1995 five people were injured when a shell hit the Ciglane outdoor market. Mr. Skrba, can you tell us what the target was then in June of 1995 in Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that the tank went into action again or the gun, and then there was a defect when the gun fired the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, you were very specific in telling us that the tank was only -- you only fired at the tank in 1992, 1993, and 1994. This is 1995.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't know that I opened fire at the time, but if anyone from the Serbian positions returned fire that was probably because of the tank or the self-propelled gun coming out of the tunnel and perhaps there was a technical error that related to the weather conditions or the gunpowder and so on and so forth. So perhaps there was something defective; however, I'm not familiar with that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But earlier in your testimony when you were talking about full preparation, the weather and the ammunition -- or excuse me, the weather conditions or the gunpowder, those are things that would be checked during full preparation - correct? - to ensure that the firing would be accurate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is checked, but if the gunpowder was wet when the weapon was being loaded, if the temperatures are high, then the shell can fall short of its target or it can be defective. It's like in the case of doctors who make mistakes. For example, they cut into tissue too deeply and then it's too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But your answer is limited to occasions of full preparation. When we spoke about simple preparation, none of this stuff was checked; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is checked. But, for example, if you have cases of ammunition and you take the top case and it was raining, then the gunpowder might be wet. So when you use that gunpowder to fire from a weapon, the conditions have changed. So in spite of the fact that you previously made checks, the shell can fall short of its target or it can overreach its target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I think we understand now the variables that go into accurate targeting. But my point is earlier today you said in terms of simple preparation none of this was done, none of this checking was done. The only thing that happened was that you had a topographical map, you had a location, and you fired to see if you were accurate. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have observers who try to see where the shell falls. This is why targeting is corrected in the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go back to the map 65 ter 23918, and now we're going to go to map 7, which is Bjelave. This is the next area that you spoke about in paragraph 18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can see from this map the streets and the roads -

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we don't need to do this in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But if you just turn the page, you'll see the satellite version of this same area. Can you describe the general nature of this area, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a civilian area, almost a hundred per cent. I think the buildings are mostly residential buildings, but some are perhaps also collectively owned buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 18 you pin-pointed this area, saying: In June 1992 there were 120-millimetre mortars that you targeted. Can you show us on this map by writing where those mortars were located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't fire on this area, I never did. You can't claim that I did. I only heard that there were mortars positioned there, but my unit never fired on them. Others did. But I heard from my colleagues, from neighbours, and so on and so forth that there were 120-millimetre mortars that were located there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll skip to the next one at paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if in e-court we can go to map 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is when you discussed city hall. And in paragraph 18 you said you received information that city hall had been turned into an ammunition dump -- depot and this was August of 1992. By looking at this map can you pin-point where city hall is or the library?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies to the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now you call this city hall in your statement, but this was the location of the library; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. The information that you received, when exactly did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps at the beginning of August, information that there were large warehouses in which ammunition was being kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the source of information was their media, the television.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You mean the source of your intelligence that it was being kept as an ammunition depot was the television?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the news on two or three occasions in the evening and you could see a lot of people walking around there carrying cases of ammunition. As to whether they were carrying them to the positions or taking them there, I don't know, but they were there in the vicinity and they were caught on camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So at the end of August there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the information you received you received at the beginning of August, but the actual shelling of the library was August 27th; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because -- let me repeat what I have said. My unit didn't shell any targets there. If other units from our army did, well, it would be normal if this caught fire on the top, but it was on fire at the bottom. So I'm wondering how that is possible. How can it be on fire at the bottom level and not at the top, especially if what we're dealing with is ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's back up. The information that you understood that it was an ammunition depot came from seeing on the television people walking around carrying cases of ammunition in the vicinity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here you have the tram lines. It wasn't working at the time, but you could see people walking around carrying these cases. This could be seen from these observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you had no further information that the actual library --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your testimony today that it was not your unit that fired at the library, it was somebody else's unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our unit wasn't assigned the task of firing on those targets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. The witness didn't say that some other unit opened fire. The witness said he doubted it was the result of shelling because the fire was ground level; the top of the building, the roof, hadn't caught fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, in any event, Ms. West, this shelling of library was stricken out from the indictment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed it was, Your Honour, but this witness speaks of it specifically in his statement so that's why I'm asking about it. In addition, putting that aside, I think it's relevant to everything that happened in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move on now?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, just one more question about the area, not the library itself. This area of the down-town -- or strike that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, would you like to tender this marked map?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you could put the date and your signature on this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this will be Exhibit P5936.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I hadn't already asked you, but can you describe the nature of this down-town area. What type of things were located there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the name of the town is a -- pretty densely populated town mostly with some 20 to 30 per cent of collective housing units. Otherwise, it's all single, individual, housing units.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we could turn to map 11, please. It's two more pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're now going to look at a map of Dobrinja. And map 11 is the one that shows the roads. And if we can just turn the page - we don't need to do this in e-court - you can see the satellite as well. Mr. Skrba, please describe the nature of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja is a new neighbourhood built before the Olympic games in 1974 and it's exclusively housing facilities with collective accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 21 of your report you spoke about scheduled incident G7 which was an incident in Dobrinja. And in that paragraph you noted that at the -- you noted that the allegation is that 120-millimetre mortars were fired at Dobrinja, and specifically you said at the battalion level there were no 120-millimetre weapons but they were in the MAD under my control in your unit, and I claim that no fire was opened that day from 120-millimetre mortars for it would have to be in the report of UNPROFOR observers who were on duty at my command post around-the-clock and would have heard firing of a shell. I want to talk about the UNPROFOR -- you called them UNPROFOR officers who were there, because in another part of your statement at paragraph 14 you said that these members were always on duty with you around-the-clock. So my question is: What was the name of the UNMO most at your command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lima 5 and they were there from the 1st of July, 1992, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that your testimony is that those military observers knew at what targets you were firing because they were posted at your command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there in the same room as me. They were on duty there for 24 hours. They slept there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that their presence had some effect on your firing, as to whether you would fire at one target or whether you would fire somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would inform them every time we fired. We never fired a shell without informing them first. They were standing there with us, sitting there, or if it was night they were sleeping there. We would be sleeping, then if -- at night I would wake up, they would wake up, and since they were sitting there with me they would hear exactly if one, two, or three shells were fired and they would record that. During those four years, they never said anything in terms of not approving or not agreeing with my reports about everything that was fired in -- during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P01426, please. And may we have page 19, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, this Court has heard evidence from senior military observer particularly about Lima 5. And beginning at page 79 he says he visited the Limas OPs. He's observed instances of what he believed to be indiscriminate fire on the city with weapons, and I'll quote. He says: "When you are at a gun site, and weapons fire, as an UNMO you are not party to the range map which the commander is using to determine his target. As a result, I always asked that my UN military observers to ask local commanders what their target was, in an attempt to determine if it was acceptable as a target or not. We were, by virtue of the system I have described, only as effective as the answer I was given by the local commander. They did not prevent us persisting in the attempt to reduce the level of tension created upon the city by reducing the numbers of rounds fired." So, Mr. Skrba, my question is this: Do you agree that the only way the military observers knew what the target was was if the commanders told them what it was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at an example of this and I'll ask you another question. If we can go on to paragraph 80. "On several occasions I personally brought such pressure to bear on the local commanders concerning firing on the city. On occasions I received answers that I regarded as unsatisfactory. I received answers that were trivial, such as the commander telling me at the Lima 5 position, when firing his mortar rounds, that he was 'warming the barrels.' I accept warming the barrels is a requirement if you have a fire mission and you then proceed with that fire mission, but the instances that I recall, the firing ceased after a few rounds, whether because of my intervention or not, I cannot determine, but it rather negated the original reason for firing the weapons in the first instance. The rationale for firing the weapon was irrational and vague; I don't think there was a specific target. On another particular occasion, I was told that the three rounds that had been fired were one for each finger of the Serb salute." Mr. Skrba, the Lima 5 position was the position at your post; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that the information the commander gave this UNMO was not very informative, was it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. I would like to face that person, if necessary, so that we can look at each other in the eye. We were sitting there together. He could see where the barrels were turned, where the fire went, and he would take the number of fired shells from me or from my deputy if I was not there. And he never made any kind of oral or written objection to these reports. I don't want to keep repeating these things. I don't want to say anything that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to paragraph 17 of your statement, and in that paragraph you talked about aerial bombs. You said: "My unit had no contact with aerial bombs nor were they used; i.e., launched in my zone on enemy military targets. Although the brigade had a number of aerial bombs on stock, they were never used in our zone of responsibility." So you concede that the brigade did have aerial bombs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "they were never used in our zone of responsibility," you're speaking about that area on the map that you indicated for one of the Defence exhibit, that entire area that was under your control?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying it was not used from that area and that the aerial bombs that existed were found by my brigade at the end of the war. They were never used. They remained in stock.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So is your testimony no aerial bombs were used out of that zone at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No aerial bombs were used as far as I know, and the ones that we had within the brigade stayed unused and were found at the end of the war because for that you would need to have special weapons, special artillery to be able to fire them, and we didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How would you describe the accuracy of an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any experience with that. I didn't do that even during my military term of office or during the war. I really never dealt with that, so I wouldn't wish to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I know you say that you never personally dealt with it, but because of your position you must have some experience, and let me ask you this: Air bombs could only be directed at a general area; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't read the instructions on their use, so I really cannot say much. I cannot answer that question. I never used them. I never prepared them for use, so I really never dealt with them and I never allowed anyone to use them in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Skrba, you'll have to forgive me but you were the commander of this artillery unit. You've conceded that the brigade had air bombs. Are you saying that you cannot in any way tell this Court now whether they were accurate weapons or inaccurate weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I didn't deal with something, didn't use it, I cannot say whether it's good or not good. You cannot say that you conducted surgery, carried out surgery, on somebody if you did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I think this subject matter might be a little bit different, so let's give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P1310, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a document dated April 1995, it's to the Main Staff. It's from the chief of artillery of the SRK. Thank you. And in the English it says: "At the morning briefing ... the decision was taken to fire on Donji Kotorac using air bombs." The second paragraph is: "The firing was supposed to be executed in the early evening hours and all the necessary prep for the firing to be executed were to have been made beforehand." But then at paragraph 3 it talks about the assessment of all the facilities in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel entrance, which in this case was the target, and he says that: "We have established through measuring carried out using instruments that two UNPROFOR points are at most 200 metres away, while the UNPROFOR observers are constantly moving from their ... stations throughout the settlement ..." And then in the next paragraph he additionally says: "Our forward defence line is ... 500 metres away from the tunnel entrance and the direction of fire is over the 'Kula' restaurant. "Because I was unable to report this information to the commander after reconnaissance, as he was in the zone of responsibility of the Igman Brigade, I have abandoned the firing on account of it jeopardising the security of our own forces and that of the UN forces." Mr. Skrba, would you agree with me that the basis of the decision to abandon fire using air bomb is because the UN were 200 metres from the target and the defence line was 500 metres from the target. Is that the basis of the decision to abandon it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who received the order to carry it out and then decided not to carry it out is the one to answer. I cannot answer that. This is something that has to do with the corps command. They have their own unit for these jobs or tasks. This is something that would be a matter for the corps and not for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you weren't behind this decision-making, but nonetheless you come to us with great experience. And my question is: Do you agree that the decision to abandon the attack was because of the concern that the air bomb's imprecision was so great that they feared their own front lines 500 metres away would be at risk?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this has already been answered. I was not permitted to push the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While I don't agree with Mr. Karadzic's intervention, but are all these questions necessary in light of timing? Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to look at one last document, P1198, on the same subject matter, however a bit closer to Mr. Skrba's area of responsibility. This is a document May 1995. It's from Dragomir Milosevic to the Ilidza Infantry Brigade and the Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, and it says on number 1: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare an aerial bomb launcher with at least five aerial bombs. The crews and launcher must be prepared to open fire at my command at any given moment (launcher roughly aimed at the airport)." On Thursday you told us that the corps command was located at Lukavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your statement you have indicated that Lukavica was your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so this is an air bomb that is going to be located within your area of responsibility, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's partly my area and partly the area of the Ilidza Brigade. It depends from where you are observing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's focus on the words in parenthesis "the launcher roughly aimed at the airport." We've talked a bit about specific targeting language. You would not consider that to be very specific, would you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aerial bombs have a lot of power. They're heavier. They have more projectiles. If a shell is heavy, some 50 or 70 kilogrammes, and if the aerial bomb is heavy from 3- to 500 kilogrammes, of course it has a lot of lethal power, a lot of destructive power, and of course one cannot be sure to hit the centre. If you fire a shell and then you can vouch for hitting the target within 50 metres, in the case of an aerial bomb it would be 500 metres because it's much -- it's much bigger projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Notwithstanding your enthusiastic denial of knowing anything about aerial bombs, you've just told us that they're heavier, they have more projectiles, and if you fire a shell and you can vouch for hitting the target within 50 metres, but in the case of an aerial bomb it would be 500 metres. So are you saying that the potential range of area is 500 metres for an aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If you hit within 50 metres, then you have a good shot. I'm not saying it's the precision of the fire is within 50 metres. If you hit within 50 metres, it's good, then that's that. If you have a 3- to 500 kilogramme bomb, it's clear, you don't have to see it or hear it to know that it has more lethal power and that its range or its impact area is greater. I mean, this is quite clear. Again I'm saying here, I did see aerial bombs but I never participated in preparing or firing one so I really cannot know the specifics of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few, Your Excellency, and if I manage to put short questions and get short answers it's not going to take that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skrba, do you know approximately how many mosques there were in Sarajevo? You don't have to give us a precise number?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost 200, 180 to 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were they active, were they being used for gathering --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does this transpire from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it transpires because there was a question if they avoided hitting places where people would assemble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were all those mosques active and were they used for people assembling, sometimes even five times a day for the five prescribed prayers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for those mosques that were at the front line facing our positions, they were not active; but along the depth of the area, they were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in 1.200 days they would have met at least 6.000 times, those mosques would have been full of people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact number, but it is a large number because Ramadan was celebrated throughout those four years there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many shells did you fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked how many mosques did you hit. The answer is good but in the question the "mosque" is missing.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not hit any mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that in mid-August 1994 NATO -- in mid-August 1994 did NATO shell our positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should have rose more quickly, but these questions should be open-ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown an order here, a preparatory order, to fire at Igman and Saracko [phoen] Polje for the 14th of August. Are you able to tell us what happened on the 14th of August and were those areas the city -- were those areas considered to be the city centre or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igman and the area towards Vojkovici and Hrasnica is not a populated area, it was not an inhabited zone at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that General Sefer Halilovic's apartment was in Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the explosion in his balcony, was that ascribed to the Serbs and then the general managed to prove that it was not the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I know Mr. Karadzic is new to redirect, but he understands that the questions cannot be like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Really, I will need a little bit of time to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to General Halilovic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know during the war, but after the war I found out from some programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Chamber briefly what that was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions I watched programmes on federal television and he said that he knew more or less who did that and that he should have been liquidated in that apartment and not his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serbian side, did it place its heavy weapons in civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslim side do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes they did. There's an example that we discussed around Bjelave, this is a populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't the Serb side do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were afraid of retaliation, of causing a reaction and causing more victims at the firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Colonel Mole, you saw his statement, was he part of the permanent crew at Lima 5?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember him. I would like to meet him and face him, particularly after a statement by him to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The entrance to the tunnel, is that a legitimate target, the tunnel -- the Dobrinja-Butmir tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a legitimate target from my area of responsibility, but we did not hit that because the tunnel was not occupied. There were civilians, soldiers passing there, supplies, fuel, medical supplies, and I just would like to note that Mr. Alija was never late for any meeting at all and he would leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the tunnel in Velesici, does that have two entrances?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the weapons that were in the tunnel, were they able to fire and did they fire from both of the entrances?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from both. I said that to the lady as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Witness, thank you very much for your being here and for your effort.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have any questions for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Skrba. On behalf of this Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, will we be reconvening in private session for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has a matter to discuss in closed session, when we resume at five past 11.00 the Chamber will start in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, Mr. President, could I request that he be given a warning pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please take a seat, Mr. Skrba. Having heard your submission as well as the parties' submission, the Chamber is not still satisfied that there exists an objectively grounded risk to your security or welfare or your family members. The Chamber finds that concerns you raised are generic, not specifically related to the fact that you will be testifying in this case, as such does not reach the level that warrants protective measures requested for. I hope you understand that. Would the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrba. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Skrba, before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal still has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other cases against you for any offence other than false testimony. Sir, do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrba. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6031 in the e-court system, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, is this the statement that you gave to -- was it read to you in English, or rather, in the Serbian language? Is this a statement that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have signed this statement, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put the same questions to you that are contained in the statement today here in the courtroom, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the answers I gave would not be in the same order, but the gist of what I said would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said as part of a package but that hasn't been included. In other words, does this include the associated documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you're tendering six documents? Any objections, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will all be admitted and given numbers by the Registrar in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read out a short summary of Mr. Skrba's testimony. I'll read it out in English. [In English] Milos Skrba lived in Pofalici. The atmosphere there was tense. Before the war the Green Berets had established a check-point where they controlled passengers and automobiles at the intersection of Drinska Street and Pofalici. Already during 1991 he saw uniformed Muslims especially in the area of Alipasino Polje. He was often stopped and controlled by the Green Berets because of which he decided to relocate with his family to a Serbian-majority area. In April 1992 he fled to the village of Petrovici near Sarajevo. After his arrival there, the local population self-organised and went out on the outskirts of the village in order to defend their houses. Also in April 1992 Muslim forces severed the only road linking Petrovici with Pale in the area of the Alatiste intersection and the Osmice feature, and in May 1992 they were forced to go out on that road and re-take it because of frequent attacks of Muslim forces and Green Berets on their patrols. In the summer 1992 the 2nd Infantry Company of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade was formed. He assumed the duty of company commander. This company was primarily responsible for preventing Muslim forces from severing the only road between Lukavica and Pale and for preventing daily threats to civilians, in particular civilian vehicles using this road. Parts of the 1st Mountain Brigade -- probably of the 10th Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps Army of BH ranged against them committed massacres of civilians in its zone of responsibility. While on guard duty his unit could often hear the moans and cries of men, women, and children during the night in the vicinity of their positions. The Muslim units had positions in-depth exclusively in civilian facilities and houses as well as snipers. Milos Skrba's company did not have heavy artillery weapons. It was a light infantry company. He never received any written or oral order from the battalion command to open fire on civilian targets, nor would he have done so had such an order ever been issued. Likewise, he never ordered orally or in writing that fire be opened on civilian targets. Regarding Markale II incident on 28th of August, 1995, Milos Skrba knows for a fact that there were no mortar positions in the village of Studenkovici which he has shown on the map 1D08529, and he showed the approximate place where there was an 92-millimetre mortar in August 1995. That is the only place on that road where there was a mortar position. He also claims that at the other positions in the vicinity there were no 120-millimetre-calibre mortars. Regarding the sniping incident in Zagrici Street on 13th of December, 1992, Milos Skrba claims that there were no sharpshooters in his company throughout 1992 as well as in December 1992 or during the entire period of the war. [Interpretation] At this point in time, the Defence doesn't have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Skrba, as you heard your evidence in this case was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I begin I just note that Mr. Karadzic accidentally read out "92-millimetre mortar." In his summary and I believe he meant 82-millimetre in August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I will be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like the Registrar to call up, please, 1D05827A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skrba, while that's coming up, I want to ask you a few questions about your evidence regarding the defence of Serbian houses in the village of Petrovici. And your statement at paragraph 3 you said that: "The local population self-organised and went out on the outskirts of this Serbian village in order to defend their houses." And you marked on the map the line of defence of Serbian houses. Now, if we could look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Again, that's not been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is one of the associated exhibits from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you put A at the end of the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The Defence put A at the end of the exhibit number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's now on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the one without A is on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let's work with that one for the moment, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, what's coming up is the first map that you marked with a red line, which you claim relates to the defence -- the line of defence of Serbian houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until we have the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could zoom in on the bottom right corner of this map, please. That's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I think we can see a straight red line which you marked in -- on this map. Is that right, Mr. Skrba?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: That's not the map. This is a different map that relates to a different case. There's a map that looks a little different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, it's correct, isn't it, that you did mark one map with one red line and later you marked another map with a red line in a different location, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: I didn't mark this map with this line. I don't know who did. This line relates to the Studenkovici village where these mortars were allegedly located. It has nothing to do with the defence of Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that - and I'm actually seeing it - the map with number A, shall we upload that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. For the record, this is in fact the map referred to at paragraph 3 of the witness statement which is map 1D8527. And now keeping in mind the location of that red line, if we can look at 1D8527A. Again, Mr. Registrar, if you could focus on the -- that's perfect. In fact, if we could include the word "Sarajevo" on the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you can confirm, can you, that this is a map which you marked showing the line of defence of Serbian houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now on this map the village of Petrovici is not, in fact, marked. Could you take a pen and approximately identify where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until assisted by our usher, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main road runs in this direction Pozarevici. Petrovici is somewhere here behind Kozarevici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak up a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Kozarevici and then Petrovic. That is the street here. In this area there are three villages: Miljevici, Gojkovici, Kozarevici, and Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you just put the letter P next to the location of Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly because it's covered by this box, this inbox here, but if there is some other map I could use that. It would be roughly speaking here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could sign and date --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: This is approximate. I'm not certain because I'm not sure that this is the actual location. So I have marked it approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sign and date the map.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: I apologise, it's the 21st, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 22nd I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5937, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you explain why you changed the position of the red line between the first map that we saw and the second map that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Because I didn't know who marked the map. I didn't and those weren't the positions, in fact, they were patrols there in May and April 2002 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there were no guards, there were patrols because the Territorial Defence was there and the guards were on duty there to prevent the Muslim units from infiltrating the villages of Miljevici and Petrovici because they were -- that was a joint village so it was an area of strategic importance and the desire was to prevent an attack on Miljevici, Petrovici, and Kozarevici and this other village Gojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you accept that the red line on your map is not, in fact, on the outskirts of Petrovici?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, practically it's not far from the village of Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, we'll be seeing exactly where the village of Petrovici is located a bit later on, Mr. Witness. I'm going to move on now. I'd like you to -- you can refer to it if you wish, at paragraph 11 of your statement you say: "In my company there were no sharpshooters throughout 1992 as well as in December 1992 or during the entire period of the war."

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, your company was in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You accept that your company was a subordinate unit of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade distributed sniper rifles to its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't get anything as the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
